web_evidence.title: Review of The Scapegoat - Laura Varnam
web_evidence.note: This estate-hosted literary review identifies the Englishman John as the novel’s narrator, quotes his first-person opening, and follows the same narrator through the final chapter.

web_evidence.title: The Art of Uncertainty: Narrative Strategies in the Fiction of Daphne du Maurier
web_evidence.note: Caroline S. Denhez’s Concordia University thesis explicitly classifies The Scapegoat among novels using a masculine first-person narrator and identifies John as its narrator.

web_evidence.title: Foreign Affairs, by Avril Horner and Sue Zlosnik
web_evidence.note: The displayed academic chapter states explicitly that The Scapegoat is a first-person narrative with a male narrator and identifies that narrator as John.

web_evidence.title: The Scapegoat - Daphne du Maurier - Google Books
web_evidence.note: The publisher-authorized book record displays a short first-person passage in which John encounters his double; its brevity limits it to corroborating the opening.

search_log: Searched “The Scapegoat” with Daphne du Maurier plus excerpt, first chapter, narrator, point of view, and first person; opened the Google Books record and the Virago publisher page.
The Virago “Read Excerpt” control resolved back to the product page, so it did not provide a sustained excerpt usable as Tier A evidence.
Opened Laura Varnam’s full estate-hosted review, which identifies John as narrator and discusses the narrative from its opening through its ending.
Searched scholarly sources and opened Caroline S. Denhez’s Concordia University thesis and the Horner–Zlosnik chapter listing, both explicitly describing the novel’s first-person male narration.
Ran targeted searches for alternating narration, multiple narrators, epistolary form, and frame narrative; found no credible evidence of a sustained change away from John’s first-person narration.
person_note: The event quotations repeatedly expose John as the participating “I” narrator across action, reflection, travel, and château scenes. Dialogue and gnomic quotations are local material, while third-person descriptions without a narratorial marker are unmarked rather than evidence for third person; two heavily clipped fragments remain unclear. Independent Tier B structural sources explicitly describe the whole novel as a first-person narrative told by John, and the estate-hosted review traces that narrator from the opening through the ending. No credible alternating, framed, or epistolary structure was found. The only remaining limitation is the lack of an accessible sustained publisher excerpt, but the broad quote evidence and multiple whole-book scholarly descriptions independently agree.
